World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Water and sewage bill increases on the way for Tasmanians
World.content:
Water bills for Tasmanian households and small businesses will rise by an average of 5.7 per cent each year for the next four years, after the Economic Regulator handed down a decision on TasWater's pricing structure.

It means an estimated average increase of $80 for households in 2026–27, taking the yearly bill to $1,487.

For tenants, who cannot be passed on the fixed component of the bill, the average yearly cost will rise by $25, with small businesses hit by an increase of $172.

By 2030, customers would pay up to 25 per cent more than in 2026, as opposed to 40 per cent under TasWater's original proposal.

Last year, TasWater applied to the regulator for an 11.5 per cent average increase over the period, sparking outcry from community groups, the state government and the opposition.

In a draft determination released in February this year, regulator Joe Dimasi knocked that back — instead proposing 4.3 per cent.

At the time, he said it was "not prudent" for TasWater to attempt all of the infrastructure works it was looking to fund through customer increases.

Original 'high burden' plan dismissed

When announcing the 5.7 per cent increase today, Mr Dimasi said he had taken a "revised approach" and that updated inflation interest rate forecasts had also affected the final decision.

However, he maintained his criticism of TasWater's original infrastructure investment plans.

"Most Tasmanians appear to understand the need for investment, but TasWater's proposal would have placed a very high burden on households and local businesses at a time when cost‑of‑living pressures are already significant."

In its original pricing proposal, TasWater had planned a $1.67 billion infrastructure program. It will instead be given a $1.18 billion allowance.

Mr Dimasi also said there had been an "unprecedented level of public engagement" on the pricing proposal and that he had received 102 submissions.

" I would like to thank everyone who took the time to make a submission and share their views. "

TasWater reviewing decision

A spokesperson for TasWater said in a statement that the company welcomed the final determination.

"Our focus now is on understanding what the decision means for our customers, communities and the services we deliver," they said.

"We're carefully reviewing the detail and will share further information once that work is complete."

For renters, who cannot be passed on the fixed component of the bill, the average yearly cost will rise by $25. (Unsplash: ManuelTheLensman)

The utility, which is jointly owned by local councils and the state government, expressed disappointment in February with the Economic Regulator's draft 4.3 per cent decision.

Chief financial officer Kane Ingham told reporters that delaying the planned works, which focused on aging sewerage assets, would risk waterway closures.

"We feel really strongly that now is the time to address these issues, otherwise we risk placing these problems on future Tasmanian generations, most likely at a greater cost and greater consequence," he said.

Labor Treasury spokesperson Dean Winter said the party "congratulates the Economic Regulator for rejecting TasWater's ridiculous proposal", calling for dividends paid to council to be kept in check.

Sewage charges to change

Currently, TasWater customers pay a fixed charge for sewage, a fixed charge for water and then a variable charge for the amount of water they use.

The economic regulator has allowed TasWater to begin charging a variable charge for the amount of sewage.

It will start at 22 cents per kilolitre of sewage in 2026–27, before rising to 27 cents by 2029–30.

TasWater had also proposed changing the tariff structure to make variable charges form a greater proportion of a customer's bill.

The Economic Regulator says it is generally supportive of that move as it would "encourage efficient water use", but that more work is needed.

He found that TasWater "had not yet demonstrated that its proposed pricing structures were sufficiently supported by robust cost modelling, transparent methodologies, or comprehensive analysis of customer impacts."

Under the approved structure, fixed charges would decrease from around 85 per cent of a bill in 2025–26 to 81 per cent in 2029–30.

World.title: SA premier defends course development despite LIV Golf doubts
World.content:
South Australia's premier says a controversial $45 million redevelopment of the North Adelaide golf course is still worth pursuing despite major doubts about the future of LIV Golf.

Peter Malinauskas has compared the project to a similar investment at Barossa Park which hosted two AFL Gather Round matches in 2025 and 2026 after Lyndoch oval was upgraded.

In February last year, the state government announced a major upgrade of the North Adelaide course on the presumption it would host future LIV Golf tournaments.

Overnight, there have been further reports that Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund was preparing to pull finances from LIV Golf and a planned event in the US was postponed.

Mr Malinauskas said he had spoken to LIV Golf's chief executive Scott O'Neil last Monday after speculation about the future of the Saudi-funded tournament.

Premier Peter Malinauskas speaking to the media at Barossa Park on Thursday. (ABC News)

However, he said he had no more information beyond what he had read in the media.

"Needless to say, we are monitoring it very closely and naturally we always assess our options," the premier said on Thursday afternoon.

" We'll wait and see how things play out in the coming days. "

He said Mr O'Neil had assured him Adelaide was still scheduled to host LIV Golf at Kooyonga Golf Club next year.

"They made it very clear they're committed to the future, including the 2027 event in Adelaide," he said.

"Now we haven't received any official position otherwise since then."

LIV Golf previously committed to staying in Adelaide until 2031. (ABC News)

'Public asset' for community

During a press conference at Lyndoch, Mr Malinauskas outlined comparisons between the North Adelaide golf course and Barossa Park.

While the Barossa Park project has been largely uncontroversial and the centre is used by local sporting groups in the 51 weeks the AFL is not playing games there, there have been protests at the North Adelaide golf course, mainly because it will involve cutting down about 600 trees in the park lands.

Mr Malinauskas said the new North Adelaide golf course would similarly be open to the public, and that golf was more likely to attract tourists throughout the year.

"The truth is the same opportunity is before us at North Adelaide and that is why the government has committed to invest in a public, community sports facility that every week of the year will be available for the South Australian public to use and in the event that we have major tournaments we can use it to promote our city and our state," he said.

A protester against the North Adelaide golf course redevelopment. (ABC News: Angelique Donnellan)

Last February, Mr Malinauskas said LIV Golf committing to play at North Adelaide from 2028–2031 justified the investment in the golf course.

"We didn't want to invest heavily in North Adelaide and face the prospect of it being lost from South Australia," he said.

"This gives us the security that it requires to be able to justify that investment."

On Thursday, he said the project remained worthwhile.

"We believe that there is a strong case for making an investment into a public asset for the people of the state, but particularly considering that it will be a drawcard for tourists in the heart of our city year-round week-in, week-out regardless of whether or not there's a tournament there."

The state government took control of the North Adelaide golf course from the Adelaide City Council on Monday and work has already started on the ground.

Trees are expected to be cut down as part of the North Adelaide golf course redevelopment. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Call for work to stop

The opposition and the Greens have each said work on the North Adelaide golf course should stop, with Liberal leader Ashton Hurn urging for the funds to be used elsewhere.

"Without having an event like LIV Golf, it's hard to see how $45 million is justifiable," Ms Hurn said.

"This is taxpayer funds at a time where we've got record debt in South Australia, we've got emergency departments right across regional SA that are closing, and people are crying out for cost-of-living relief."

Greens MLC Robert Simms said it was not too late for the government to change course and "stop the chop".

"The business case for this redevelopment has totally evaporated," Mr Simms said.

World.title: Chalmers does little to quell CGT debate as budget looms
World.content:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

If Jim Chalmers needed a reminder that he's running out of time to revamp the budget, the countdown clock quietly ticking on the treasury website is a sight for sore eyes.

The treasurer has been pretty clear the budget he's handing down in two weeks isn't the one he dreamed up originally. But "there are some common elements", he told a CommBank podcast.

Favoured buzzwords like "intergenerational fairness" and "resilience and reform" have been used so much in recent weeks they've begun to lose all meaning (perhaps if you say it three times fast, the treasurer will be summoned like Beetlejuice).

The framing has also started to look at the question of whether young people not getting a "fair crack" at the housing market could be a threat to social cohesion. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used the argument when asked about whether the government was about to move on negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount.

Resilience wasn't just about us being prepared for global shocks (say, through more money being set aside for fuel security), he argued, but also about "giving people a sense of ownership over the economy".

If reports are to be believed (the same ones the government hasn't gone out of its way to correct), the May 12 budget is expected roll back the 50 per cent CGT discount for assets held for more than 12 months — potentially reverting back to the pre-1999 system.

Loading...

Seven years ago, proposed changes to CGT and negative gearing were named as part of the reason Labor lost the unlosable election. But as the cliche goes, a week is a long time in politics: 2019 might as well be another lifetime.

Chalmers all but confirmed it would be at least partially grandfathered, while also playing down expectations it would result in an increase in revenue.

"Without getting into hypotheticals about policies, what you try and do is to make sure that we recognise the decisions that people have taken in the past," he told the same CommBank podcast.

The budget isn't finished. Uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz is making it hard to forecast just how high inflation will rise. Inflation rose to 4.6 per cent in March, the Australian Bureau of Statistics confirmed. That's likely to rise higher but by how much is anyone's guess.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

So, this budget must be a little bit everything, everywhere all at once — responding to the Iran war, to inflation, to the need for big reform.

There's a term in realty television: the frankenbite. That's when producers cut two soundbites together to make a new sentence. You can't escape the feeling that this budget feels like one big frankenbite.

However, the idea the government was flirting with any form of gas export tax in this budget has been put to bed. Proponents were briefly confident that the prime minister's language meant it was still on the table in the future.

But as Foreign Minister Penny Wong has been in Asia for talks with China, South Korea and Japan about strengthening the region's "shared energy security", it seems unlikely that Albanese has any appetite to move there.

DJ Tim makes a playlist

Tim Wilson has had a rough start to his time as shadow treasurer. And things didn't get any easier this week after he inflated the price tag of the Coalition's fuel reserve scheme from $800 million to $80 billion.

After first trying to justify the price tag when the opposition has been so vocal with its criticism of the government's spending, reporters pressed on. Wilson later corrected himself.

The price tag to double Australia's minimum fuel reserves was already ambiguous.

The actual cost to boost Australia's storage facilities would be around $6 billion, so the $800 million was simply a contribution. The rest would have to be paid by the facilities themselves, which would likely pass that onto drivers at an estimated cost of 1 cent per litre.

Tim Wilson curated his own budget playlist this week. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A day later, Wilson offered up a playlist for Chalmers to listen to as he prepared the budget, which included You're So Vain and Dolly Parton's Baby I'm Burnin'. Chalmers responded by calling Wilson, who previously sang a parody version of We Didn't Start the Fire in Parliament House, a "karaoke clown".

Of course, this is all small-fry stuff. But this newsletter couldn't escape the temptation to offer up a few additions of its own: Paramore's Hard Times, Price Tag by Jessie J, Taylor Swift's Don't Blame Me, and Begin Again (really, I could have done this whole thing based on Swift alone).

Loading

PM calls for report not to be politicised

Meanwhile, the antisemitism royal commission handed down its interim report. It made 14 recommendations, including five that haven't been released. Some of the redacted material could be released after the criminal proceedings conclude. The others will likely remain sealed as they contain national security information.

Antisemitism royal commission delivers first report The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion has released its interim report, making 14 recommendations.

Albanese convened a national security committee of cabinet to consider the findings and adopted all the recommendations that apply to the Commonwealth.

A recommendation to update the national firearms agreement will only boost the federal government's efforts to revive its ambition to implement its proposed gun buyback scheme. Albanese's March deadline has come and gone.

Albanese invoked Port Arthur (this week also marked 30 years since the mass shooting) as he urged the holdout states to come on board.

"There was no politicisation of any of those events. And to the credit of John Howard, Tim Fischer and Kim Beazley, the parliament acted in a way that was appropriate, and the nation is safer because of that. And I, again, would reiterate a constructive call for states and territories to work with the Commonwealth," he said.

Public hearings for the royal commission start next week in Sydney.

World.title: Trucking industry calls for tougher penalties for dangerous overtaking
World.content:
Western Australian truck drivers are outraged by the light penalties people receive for overtaking dangerously or crossing continuous lines.

Truck driver Ben Sutherland finds the behaviour of some drivers on country roads "unfathomable".

The long-distance driver, who is also the president of the Livestock and Rural Transporters Association, says he is confronted by appalling driving behaviour every day, especially dangerous overtaking, and he's had enough.

Ben Sutherland says he is confronted by appalling driving behaviour every day.

"It's unfathomable some of the incidents that you see on the road," he said.

"And the amount of near misses and near fatalities that we avoid every day from being on the road from stupidity and impatience."

What particularly incenses him is the relatively low maximum penalties that can be imposed for dangerous overtaking, and he is calling on the road safety minister to create a targeted campaign to change dangerous overtaking behaviour.

Loading...

The calls come after a 21-year-old woman was charged with reckless driving after dash cam video emerged of her allegedly trying to overtake a triple road train in an "unsafe and reckless manner".

Truck driver and owner of educational program for Steering the Future, Glen 'Yogi' Kendall, said the current punishments were "terrible".

"We're [truck drivers] sick of it," he said.

He said the near misses by cars trying to overtake put a huge mental stress on truck drivers.

"The road is our workplace," Mr Kendall said.

WA driving penalties vary

UWA road safety researcher Paul Roberts said that compared to other states, WA sat on the lower middle spectrum of fines.

"We're actually higher for some things and very low for other things," he said.

"Low-level speeding springs to mind. In WA, the penalties are very, very low.

"I think we're pretty much the lowest in Australia."

Offence Penalty Crossing continuous dividing lines $150 + 3 demerit points Failing to overtake at a safe distance $400 + 4 demerit points Drink driving 0.05-0.08 blood alcohol level (BAC) $1000 + up to 5 demerit points Drink driving 0.08 + (penalties for first offences) Up to $3750 + potential disqualification of licence

Dr Roberts said there was a relationship between the level of penalties and positive road safety outcomes.

"It's not just about penalties … enforcement presence, and that's really really important," he said.

"I mean, the deterrent effect is also from the probability of actually getting caught as well as the level of the fine."

A WA government website offers advice on overtaking road trains, urging drivers to be patient when passing the vehicles, which can be up to 60 metres long.

"It can take some time to safely overtake a road train, so take your time and stay several car lengths behind the truck," it reads.

A road train is dangerous to overtake, particularly on regional roads. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"When it is safe to pass, indicate, move over the centre lane, accelerate to the posted speed limit, and overtake sensibly."

In December last year, the Cook government announced an $80 million road safety reform package, which included reviewing road traffic penalties and infringements.

The ABC understands the road safety commission has begun this review and is looking at how penalties are applied, their effectiveness in improving road safety outcomes and whether they remain appropriate and proportionate.

The road safety minister has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Apologetic insurer claims customers were not tricked in renewal notices
World.content:
When the corporate regulator accused RACQ of misleading customers with insurance renewal notices, the organisation issued an emphatic public apology.

The insurer had been sending notices that compared a customer's upcoming premium against a "last period premium" — even though that was not necessarily what that customer had actually paid.

The organisation ceased the practice and proclaimed publicly last year it "was not in keeping with our high standards".

Now though, RACQ, in the relative quiet of Federal Court filings, is defending the earlier renewal notices. The organisation has denied that the notices were misleading and downplayed the possibility the price differences in renewal notices had manipulated customer behaviour.

'Misleading' premiums spark ASIC case

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) last year sued customer-owned RACQ, one of Queensland's biggest organisations with almost 1.7 million members, about renewal premium notices covering products from home to boat and pet insurance.

The lawsuit was prompted by an ABC report detailing how offer letters were comparing a new premium for an upcoming year against a "last period premium" that was higher than what customers had actually paid.

That was because the "last period premium" could exclude details such as discounts subsequently agreed after an initial quote.

One example cited was of an RACQ customer, John Monks, receiving a renewal notice showing the "last period premium" for his Gold Coast home was $6,930.55 and new offer for "this period premium" of $7,033.57. That would appear to be a 1.5 per cent rise.

John Monks said he would leave RACQ after his premium quotes more than doubled. (ABC News: Steve Keen)

But in reality, Mr Monks had negotiated a discount and only paid $5,024.18 in the previous year. It meant the renewal price rise was actually 39.9 per cent higher.

ASIC's case alleged that at least 434,548 renewal certificates were issued between September 2019 and December 2024, where the "last period premium" did not reflect the actual amount paid.

Customers had even complained to the insurer since 2019 that the comparison was "very misleading", ASIC's lawsuit said.

RACQ complaint numbers spike RACQ has seen a spike in complaints as premiums rise and insurance claims are mishandled.

But RACQ, in defence documents obtained by the ABC, rejected the corporate regulator's allegation that the average policyholder would have believed that the "last period premium" amount was the amount they had actually paid.

RACQ maintained policyholders had known the initial premium quote, had been aware of any subsequent changes to premiums from that quote and knew why they had sought a change.

That meant any "ordinary and reasonable policyholder" would have understood the context of the "last period premium" amount listed in the renewal notice, RACQ said.

ASIC's legal reply rejected that argument. It said the renewal notices did not clarify the "last period premium" had been subject to adjustments.

Even if a customer had adjusted the pricing and received paperwork earlier on, the customer could not be reasonably expected to remember those contents or cross reference them with the "last period premium" amount on the latest renewal notice, ASIC alleged.

Changes and an apology

When the case broke last year, customer-owned RACQ revealed it had changed renewal notices to now reflect actual pricing changes.

"We are disappointed this has happened and apologise to our members as this is not in keeping with our high standards or the experience we strive to offer," it said at the time.

Still, its defence also tries blunting the impact of ASIC's allegations about pricing. ASIC had alleged that customers potentially missed out on shopping around if not given actual price comparisons.

But RACQ's defence said that renewal rates were not materially different between unaffected and affected customers.

Do you know more? Contact Liam Walsh on encrypted email or Signal. Please note end-to-end encryption is only possible with your own encrypted email system like Protonmail or Signal account.

The documents also indicate that roughly 70 per cent of the 434,548 renewal certificates had a comparison premium that was higher than what people had truly paid.

But in a majority of the affected certificates, the difference between the amounts customers actually paid and what they were told was the last period premium was less than $200, RACQ said.

RACQ maintained to the ABC that while the lawsuit is about what was listed on the renewal notice, the actual price charged to customers "at all times was correct".

"We are required to respond to ASIC's statement of claim as part of the legal process," the organisation said.

World.title: NSW Police face scrutiny over patrols of Bondi terror attack event
World.content:
NSW Police officers assigned to patrol the Hanukkah celebration targeted in the Bondi Beach terrorist attack were told they did not need to "stay the entire duration" of the event, despite members of the Jewish community fearing it was at risk.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion was established after the deadly December 14 attack, and on Thursday delivered its first 14 recommendations.

Commissioner Virginia Bell's 159-page report also examined the security arrangements for the Bondi Beach Chanukah by the Sea event, at which 15 people were killed.

The report noted the attack came amid Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) "publicly and repeatedly" drawing attention to the heightened risk of terrorism and the "disturbing escalation" of antisemitic incidents between August 2024 and the end of 2025.

Governor-General Sam Mostyn has received Commissioner Virginia Bell's interim report. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

The Chanukah by the Sea event was one of three significant Hanukkah celebrations being held on the same night, with Jewish security agency Community Security Group NSW (CSG NSW) preparing risk assessments ahead of the events.

CSG NSW told NSW Police on December 8 there was a heightened threat risk and requested police assistance "to ensure community safety" at the planned Hanukkah gatherings.

Commissioner Bell's report stated this included a request for police resources "for the entirety" of the Chanukah by the Sea event.

The CSG NSW said a NSW Police officer told them it "could not provide static resources" for Chanukah by the Sea, but mobile patrols from Eastern Suburbs Police Action Command would "check in and monitor the event".

Fifteen people were killed in the attack at Bondi Beach. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

In an email sent three days before the attack, the officers tasked with attending the event were told there was "no need to stay the entire duration, but your presence will ensure the community feel safe".

The commission's report noted three general duties officers and one supervisor were allocated to the Chanukah by the Sea event, with an officer from the Eastern Suburbs Police Area Command attending the event at "various times".

NSW Police did not produce a written risk assessment for the event, the report stated.

Significant police resources responded after the terror attack occurred, with two police officers seriously injured.

The NSW Jewish Board of Deputies, which operates CSG NSW, has been contacted for comment.

The interim report made no findings related to the security arrangements for the event, but recommended the same NSW Police procedures that already apply to Jewish High Holy Days should be implemented for other high-risk Jewish festivals and events.

'Roving' police presence

NSW Police will review the royal commission's findings and recommendations.

Mal Lanyon says there was a "roving" police presence in the area before the terror attack. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said while the report found a written risk assessment for Chanukah by the Sea event was not produced, officers had assessed possible threats to the event.

"There were police presence on that occasion, there had been a risk assessment and there were certainly roving police throughout the area on the evening," he said.

" We will learn from this incident if there are lessons to be taken away, we will implement that. "

NSW Premier Chris Minns said all recommendations related to the state government were accepted in full.

"The reality for a state government is that its highest responsibility is to protect its people and on December 14 last year, we didn't do that," he said.

"We will do everything we can to change and ensure that we confront evil and terrorism wherever it is in New South Wales."

Mr Minns did not directly respond when asked if he was satisfied by the number of police resources allocated to the Chanukah by the Sea event.

"In retrospect, if we had known what was going to happen we would have put an army down there," he said.

"It didn't happen and that's what we live with now."

Jewish community welcomes findings

NSW Jewish Board of Deputies CEO Michele Goldman said NSW Police had "significantly increased" its presence at high-risk Jewish events and locations.

"The Jewish community no longer feels safe going out and about given not just the terror attack, but harassment and intimidation across a whole range of settings," she said.

"The presence of the NSW Police has provided some level of reassurance to enable life to continue."

Yanky Super is recovering after being shot in the back during the attack. (ABC News: Danuta Kozaki)

More than 40 people were injured in the terror attack, including Jewish medical group Hatzolah volunteer Yanky Super.

He said he pressed his radio's duress alarm at 6:42pm, one minute before NSW Police notified NSW Ambulance of the attack.

Mr Super still has 300 pieces of shrapnel in his back and continues to recover from his injuries.

"It's a great job the commission has done," he said.

World.title: Australians aboard flotilla intercepted by IDF
World.content:
The Global Sumud Flotilla has been intercepted on its way to Gaza by the Israeli Defense Forces, an official tweet from the organisation says.

"In a violent raid in international waters, Israeli naval forces have intercepted, boarded, and systematically disabled various boats of the Global Sumud Flotilla," the tweet said.

Earlier on Thursday morning, the organisation reported on Telegram the boats were "approached by military speedboats, self-identified as 'israel', pointing lasers and semi-automatic weapons".

Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, also confirmed the interception in a tweet.

"Another provocative flotilla was stopped before reaching our area," Mr Danon tweeted.

The flotilla is off the coast of Greece, near Crete, according to live tracking on the organisation's website.

The flotilla made up of more than 50 boats set sail in recent weeks from Marseille in France, Barcelona in Spain and Syracuse in Italy.

Jane Salmon, the flotilla's Australian delegation media liaison, said six Australians were participating in the voyage.

She said 21 boats had been intercepted.

"Surya McEwen, Dr Bianca Pullman Webb, Ethan Floyd, Neve O'Connor and Zack Schofield were on boats that were intercepted," Ms Salmon told ABC News.

Cameron Tribe was also on one of the boats that was intercepted, she said.

The ABC asked the IDF for details of the operation, but it did not provide a specific response.

“The IDF enforces the marine security blockade on the Gaza Strip and is prepared for a range of scenarios, which it will carry out in accordance with the directions of the political echelon,” a spokesperson said.

The IDF directed all requests for further information to the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The ABC has also contacted Foreign Minister Penny Wong’s office for comment.

Greens leader Larissa Waters called the incident a "yet another shocking breach of international law by Israel".

"Foreign Minister Penny Wong must back the brave flotilla crew and fight for their release," she said on social media.

In October last year, the organisation's flotilla, which included Greta Thunberg, was intercepted by the Israeli military near the besieged Palestinian territory.

The fleet consisted of 50 small vessels carrying about 500 activists from dozens of countries.

They were attempting to deliver a symbolic amount of humanitarian aid, mainly food and medicine.

The crew members were arrested and expelled by Israel.

Israel has previously said the maritime blockade is needed to prevent Hamas from importing arms.

ABC/ Wires

World.title: Music promoter charged with cocaine, cannabis offences
World.content:
A prominent Hobart entertainment businessman has appeared in court charged with trafficking cocaine and possessing cannabis.

Brendan Fagan Self, 49, was the managing director of events company Vandemonian Touring, which hosts live music acts at venues around Tasmania.

The company has previously hosted big-name artists, including Flume and Tones and I, and staged the annual Tasmanian Wine Festival.

Vandemonian Touring also formerly operated Hobart Uni Bar on the University of Tasmania's Sandy Bay campus. The venue closed in June last year.

Mr Self appeared in Hobart Magistrates Court today, where court documents outlined allegations he trafficked cocaine in September last year and possessed cannabis in February this year.

The alleged quantities of the substances were unclear.

Mr Self is yet to enter a plea.

Brendan Fagan Self's former company also ran the now-closed Uni Bar. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) documents show another person was appointed director and secretary of Vandemonian Touring in October last year.

Mr Self was represented in court by Pip Monk, who said she was waiting on more evidence from the prosecution.

She said the defence had received some of the disclosure, including property seizure records, photographs and copies of the search warrants, but that this was "absolutely nowhere near" what was required.

Magistrate Reg Marron adjourned the case until July.

World.title: ‘Tried to build the Taj Mahal with budget for a granny flat’: Demons’ Caulfield deadline revealed
World.content:
Exclusive SportRacingAFL 2026 ‘Tried to build the Taj Mahal with budget for a granny flat’: Demons’ Caulfield deadline revealed Danny Russell April 30, 2026 — 4:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The head of the government-appointed trust that manages the site proposed for Melbourne Football Club’s Caulfield Racecourse development has criticised the Demons for wanting to build a “Taj Mahal” home base with a “budget for a granny flat”. This masthead can reveal the Demons have been given a 60-day deadline to prove they can fund the $100 million training centre or the Caulfield Racecourse Reserve Trust will look for alternative tenants. Melbourne captain Max Gawn leads the Demons on the field at the MCG. via Getty Images This follows the shock dismissal of Melbourne chief executive Paul Guerra on Tuesday after only seven months in the job. Guerra, who previously headed the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, was seen as a key figure in the Demons’ search for a new training and administration centre because of his state government connections and his role as a Racing Victoria board member.



Melbourne president Steven Smith was asked about the status of the Caulfield plans after the Guerra axing on Wednesday. “We’re getting very close on Caulfield; we’re confident on Caulfield,” said Smith, who also announced the appointment of a new club CEO, Dan Taylor. Loading However, trust chairman Sam Almaliki told this masthead the onus was on Melbourne to deliver a commitment of “funding to the project”. “The one critical piece that is beyond the trust’s role and responsibility in this is the funding required to make the project a reality,” Almaliki said.



“The critical vitamin that’s missing is ‘vitamin M’ [money], and Melbourne have not been able to deliver that to date. “The truth is, they’ve tried to build the Taj Mahal, and so far they’ve only got budget for a granny flat.” An artist’s impression of the proposed Melbourne training and administration facility at Caulfield Racecourse. A source familiar with the situation, who declined to be named because the process is confidential, said Melbourne’s memorandum of understanding with the racecourse trust was extended until June 30 this year “for Melbourne to make sure that the project is feasible and that it’s got the financial backing”. This masthead reported in June last year that Melbourne was expected to provide $15 million from cash reserves and $15 million in a fundraising drive, but needed to convince the state and federal governments and the AFL to contribute the remaining $70 million.



A Melbourne Racing Club source told this masthead the racing club (which runs the track) had been dealing with the Melbourne board and not Guerra for some time, but they did not have an issue with the former CEO.



The MRC insider, who was not authorised to speak publicly, said the racing club could not see a future in which the Demons had a home base at Caulfield. Departed Melbourne CEO Paul Guerra. Joe Armao Melbourne Football Club and the state government have been contacted for comment. The Demons had requested a longer extension to the MOU with the trust, but that was denied. “From the trust’s perspective, if the Demons in working with government and other stakeholders cannot demonstrate that Caulfield is feasible and has the financial backing needed, this project is dead in its tracks,” a source said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Guerra was appointed last April. It didn’t take long for the Demons to get buyer’s remorse Almaliki, who has been chair since the trust’s inception in 2018, wrote to Premier Jacinta Allen this week, reinstating the trust’s commitment to the project and welcoming its prioritisation by the government. “The trust continues to collaborate with the Melbourne Football Club, the state government, the Melbourne Racing Club and other stakeholders to deliver a training and administration facility for the Demons at Caulfield,” he said. “Our commitment has not changed and has been consistent. It is now up to all other parties to deliver, to make this happen. That includes the Melbourne Football Club as the party that is looking to call Caulfield home.” Almaliki would not comment on Guerra’s role while at the Demons or on the club’s decision to move him on.



He said it was the trust, with support from the previous Melbourne Racing Club administration, who first approached the Demons about relocating to Caulfield. “The trust’s interest is in delivering community benefit through improved access and activity at Caulfield for everyone,” he said. “Throughout the journey, we’ve taken every opportunity to remove any obstacles in the way of making this possible. “The one outstanding component that nobody has been able to deliver is a commitment of funding to the project. And really the onus rests on the Demons to deliver that. Everything else can be worked through.” The source said the trust asked the Demons and then CEO Gary Pert late in 2024 to start building football fields inside the racecourse to show their commitment to the project, and to prove their intent to potential donors.

World.title: Paramedics ‘scared to go to work’ after colleague attacked
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Paramedics ‘scared to go to work’ after colleague attacked Alexander Darling April 30, 2026 — 4:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paramedics in Victoria are in shock after a passer-by stabbed one of their colleagues in the face and neck while he was on duty on Thursday. The victim, a 20-year professional originally from the Northern Territory, is in Royal Melbourne Hospital’s emergency department in a serious but stable condition after the incident, which happened in Melbourne’s north about 11.20am. Ambulance Victoria chief executive Jordan Emery addressed the media with union secretary Danny Hill (right) and other paramedics on Thursday. Alexander Darling Police and Ambulance Victoria said the first responder was getting coffee at a cafe in Reservoir just after 11am, when a man got out of a red car and stabbed him. The man then fled in the same car, they said. Police made an arrest in the same suburb a few hours later.



The paramedic’s injuries were not life-threatening, but Ambulance Victoria chief executive Jordan Emery said that made the situation no less serious. Related Article Exclusive

Crime ‘An absolute let-down’: Paramedics furious over assault law loophole Speaking outside the Royal Melbourne Hospital on Thursday afternoon, Emery said: “It is completely unacceptable that those people who spend their lives caring for others, who give so much to care for their communities, continue to face violence on a daily basis. “We need to spend time in our communities reflecting on how we have come to a place where more than 1000 paramedics are assaulted every single year in Victoria.” He said the problem was increasing across Victoria and that drug and alcohol abuse weren’t the only explanations.



“There will be paramedics tonight who will be scared to go to work, and rightly so, because of this appalling violence,” he said. Emery said a bystander had intervened to stop the offender, which allowed the paramedic to perform first aid on himself – despite bleeding profusely – until his colleagues arrived. “We extend our sincere gratitude and thanks to that bystander,” Emery said. “We hope that we get the opportunity to provide a more fulsome thanks directly.” Police arrested a 32-year-old man over the incident at a different street in Reservoir at 1pm. The man is being interviewed. Since 2018, injuring an emergency worker has been a category 1 offence in Victoria, meaning courts must impose a prison sentence – in this case at least six months – for those found guilty. The maximum penalty for this crime is five years in jail.



Danny Hill, secretary of Victoria’s Ambulance Union, said the incident demonstrated the need for the state’s leaders to take action. “Until it stops, we’re going to keep advocating for improvements to laws, tighter penalties, harsher penalties,” he said, though he declined to detail what these desired improvements were when asked. More to come Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The tuna chilli sanger (with hash brown) that’s autumn’s best comfort food
World.content:
Eating outSandwich Watch The tuna chilli sanger (with hash brown) that’s autumn’s best comfort food You’ll have to negotiate the Upper Mount Gravatt backstreets, crisscrossing the highway a couple of times, to find one. But boy is it worth it. Matt Shea April 30, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The most popular sandwich at Sincerity at Jacorey? Co-owner Corey Park dutifully points at the menu on the counter: the ebi katsu sando, he suggests. Or perhaps the bulgogi sando. Or maybe it’s the chilli karaage sando. All are a hit with Sincerity’s regular clientele. I’m here to tell you, though, that Sincerity’s regular clientele are wrong – if only a little bit. Sincerity by Jacorey’s chilli tuna mayo sandwich Markus Ravik All are fine sandwiches that I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend. Still, they’re all outshone by a chilli tuna mayo number that’s this autumn’s best comfort food. Here’s why. Actually, first, a little about Sincerity by Jacorey



Park and partner Jamie Kim opened their first cafe, Jacorey Dessert Cafe, in early 2024 and soon followed it with Sincerity by Jacorey. Park tends to work front of house on the coffee machine, while Kim oversees the kitchen. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article Riverside Italian classic rebooted for new generation The early focus at both cafes was handcrafted desserts such as a range of Basque cheesecakes, alongside cream lattes and iced matcha. It was only later that Kim developed a range of savoury sandwiches. They’ve since become some of the two cafes’ best-selling items. Sincerity by Jacorey is in Upper Mt Gravatt and is a funny spot to get to. It’s slotted into the ground floor of a pair of apartment blocks perched half a block back from the intersection of Logan and Kessells roads. To get there, you jump off the M1 at Klumpp Road and then wend your way through the backstreets, crossing the freeway a couple of times. Sincerity by Jacorey occupies a comfortably nondescript spot beneath an apartment building in Upper Mount Gravatt. Markus Ravik



It’s an unusual location but a pleasant one, protected from the traffic that thunders along Logan Road. Outside, there are a few tables gathered around a garden bed; the inside is dominated by a communal timber table, with counter seating looking out through floor to ceiling windows. Sincerity by Jacorey’s chilli tuna mayo sandwich What initially attracted us to this brilliant sandwich was – counterintuitively, perhaps – its relative practicality when compared to its more Instagrammable stablemates (the ebi katsu, in particular, is a real peacock of a sanger). But that restraint makes sense when Kim tells you how it came about. Inside Sincerity by Jacorey. Markus Ravik “I have this vivid memory of a spicy tuna [toastie] my sister once made,” she says. “Even though I usually can’t handle spicy food, it was that perfect kind of addictive spicy. I’ve been craving it lately so I decided to recreate it using our chewy sando bread.”



This thing is far more than a tuna toastie, though. Kim mixes skipjack tuna with kewpie mayo and a bunch of spices to create the silky chilli tuna mix at the heart of the sandwich (“[Skipjack] has richer flavour and better texture than albacore,” she says). That’s layered into the sandwich with rocket, honey mustard, tasty cheese and, most importantly, a piping hot Edgell hash brown that Kim chose for its crisp outer shell. The chilli tuna mayo sandwich alongside some of the cafe’s other popular sangers. Markus Ravik Then there’s the sando bread that the ingredients come slapped between, which Kim chose after testing “countless” other brands. She won’t be drawn on where she gets it from but says its “chewy but soft” texture provides the sandwich’s punctuation mark, especially when lightly toasted as it is here. The perfect comfort food



Yes, this thing has way more going on than that toastie Kim’s sister made all those years ago, but the DNA is the same. It’s brilliant, soul-warming comfort food. Its combination of texture and flavour, and then the interplay of temperature, so thoughtful and precise it’s like you’re sitting in on Kim’s own nostalgia. It’s manageable – you can eat it in one hand – but I often find myself eating it with two, elbows on the table, much like I used to when sitting at the kitchen counter as a kid, lost in daydreams. World.content:
NationalNSWRoads All the permanent changes coming to one of Sydney’s busiest motorways Cindy Yin April 30, 2026 — 4:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Sydney’s busiest and most complicated roads will undergo a major route shakeup, permanently changing how people move through the near-complete transport corridor connecting the city’s northern suburbs to the CBD. More than 250,000 motorists who use the Warringah Freeway each day will be affected by permanent route changes when they begin from 6am on Saturday. Southbound motorists driving to the city will need to choose either the Harbour Bridge or Harbour Tunnel lanes about 1 kilometre earlier in their journey; they will have to keep left for the bridge and right for the tunnel. The Warringah Freeway is used by more than 250,000 motorists a day. Janie Barrett The four-kilometre Warringah Freeway is one of Sydney’s busiest transport corridors and has been undergoing a $2 billion upgrade since 2022. It will allow motorists to bypass the CBD when the Western Harbour Tunnel opens in late 2028. The 6.5-kilometre project will link the WestConnex motorway under the inner west to the Warringah Freeway in the north.



The complex facelift involves balancing the amount of work that can be carried out with traffic changes such as reduced lanes and temporary ramp closures causing delays and congestion for motorists forced to divert. The final decision point heading southbound on the Warringah Freeway is moving one-kilometre further north. Transport for NSW About 17 of 300 traffic configurations remain before the project is complete at the end of this year. The permanent slip lane closure connecting the southbound Harbour Tunnel lanes to the Harbour Bridge is among the changes to be rolled out this Saturday, which means motorists can no longer cross from the inner freeway lanes to the outer lanes to avoid entering the Harbour Tunnel. The Ernest Street on-ramp’s access to the Harbour Bridge will be removed to become a dedicated entry point for the Harbour Tunnel. Access to the bridge will continue on Brook Street, Miller Street, Falcon Street, and Mount Street.



Views from the Ridge Street bridge of work on the Warringah Freeway. Sam Mooy Transport for NSW coordinator-general Howard Collins advised motorists to “keep calm”, as it would “take a while to learn those new routes”. The Falcon Street and Military Road interchange will redirect traffic to the western on-ramp for access to the bridge or tunnel, while the eastern on-ramp will become a dedicated bus lane, with no access to the Cahill Expressway or Alfred Street off-ramp. Related Article Roads ‘Like a giant game of Tetris’: Rebuilding one of Australia’s busiest motorways cone by cone NSW Minister for Roads Jenny Aitchison said the upgrades were designed to “stop weaving that has happened for decades, ensuring that once people get in, they continue in that lane throughout their journey”.



Another feature is a dedicated 2.2-kilometre bus lane running south of the Miller Street overpass to the bridge and CBD, which Aitchison said would deliver a more efficient journey for 150,000 daily bus passengers. The upgrade has attracted criticism from North Sydney Council Mayor Zoe Baker, who called the upgrade a “misconceived project”. “It’s just going to change where the congestion is, rather than address the underlying issue. It will still ultimately hit the pinch point on the Harbour Bridge and the Harbour Tunnel, and the fear is that it will encourage congestion on local roads and rat runs as previous access is cut off,” she said. World.title: Dalaroo snaps up full control of Greenland rare earths prize
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Dalaroo snaps up full control of Greenland rare earths prize Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward April 30, 2026 — 4:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dalaroo Metals has just ticked off a major milestone at its Blue Lagoon critical minerals project in south-west Greenland, successfully acquiring full control of its core exploration licence, which hosts the majority of the project. Formal grant of the tenement has now provided the company with total security over the most prospective zones of a district-scale system that has already served up high-grade rare earth elements, zirconium, niobium and hafnium. Additionally, the company has applied for massive extensions to its offshore ground that it hopes will lock up the entire mineralised system. Dalaroo Metals has secured full ownership of the high-grade heart of its Blue Lagoon project in Greenland. Dalaroo’s newly secured ground hosts a confirmed 2.7-kilometre mineralised strike, where a standout maiden field campaign in 2025 delivered anomalous values from every one of the 113-sample taken. Peak surface assays reached 0.81 per cent total rare earth oxides, a result made even more compelling by its high-value composition. Crucially, between 25 and 29 per cent of that total consists of high-demand magnet rare earth oxides.



‘By securing this core ground we are effectively controlling the entire mineral system.’ Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan Notably neodymium and praseodymium, underlining Blue Lagoon’s potential to host a significant critical minerals deposit in a premier, Western-aligned jurisdiction. Dalaroo says the transition from application to granted status is a pivotal de-risking event that offers the legal and operational runway to fast-track its upcoming field season. Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan said: “The formal grant of MEL 2022-07 is a pivotal de-risking event for Dalaroo. It provides us with 100% tenure security over the high-grade heart of the Blue Lagoon Project.” The company now effectively controls the very heart of a mineral system that it believes extends from primary source rocks on land into downstream depositional traps offshore. This “source-to-sink” model views the landscape as a natural sluice box, where constant weathering of upstream alkaline rocks releases valuable minerals into the lagoon.



While Greenland is currently taking centre stage, Dalaroo is maintaining a high-octane exploration engine at its Bondoukou gold project in Côte d’Ivoire. The company recently wrapped up a massive 2250-sample soil geochemistry program as part of its “Priority 1” phase. The campaign covered a 4.5-kilometre stretch of a formidable 9.5-kilometre gold corridor at the Gold Ridge prospect, located within the prolific Birimian Greenstone Belt. Field crews have now moved into a second priority area in the project’s northwestern block to continue the 4400-sample campaign. The systematic work aims to define high-conviction drill targets. The campaign follows up on historical rock chip samples that returned up to 17.95 grams per tonne gold. Additionally, Dalaroo has completed channel sampling at its Dingbi artisanal site to guide future drilling beneath existing surface workings. Dalaroo is also keeping boots on the ground back on home soil. At its Namban project in Western Australia’s northern wheatbelt, the company is chasing nickel, copper and platinum group elements. Notably, the project sits within the same geological setting as Chalice Mining’s massive 30-million-ounce palladium equivalent Julimar discovery, located just 80 kilometres to the south. Meanwhile, at the Lyons River project in the Gascoyne region, the company is hunting a diverse mineral bounty across an expansive 838-square-kilometre holding, with gold leading the charge. With the core Greenland tenure now locked in, Dalaroo has launched a structured de-risking program for the 2026 field season. The multi-pronged campaign will feature maiden drilling designed to define coherent mineralised zones alongside a suite of high-tech geophysical tools.



Specialised ground-penetrating radar will be deployed to map sediment thickness and identify buried “paleochannels” that could act as heavy mineral traps. In the lagoon itself, the company plans to use side-scan sonar for bathymetry and Van Veen grab sampling to retrieve seabed sediments for mineralogical analysis. By consolidating its hold on the high-grade core and simultaneously applying for massive offshore extensions, Dalaroo is acquiring the ground to potentially define a major new critical minerals province. With a 2026 exploration blitz about to kick off and as the scramble to secure the rare earths for permanent magnets continues, the company’s Greenland discovery is looking more and more like very well-timed piece of potential “company making” geological detective work. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Police mark another wanding milestone with operation in city mall
World.content:
Perspective NationalQueenslandQueensland Police Police mark another wanding milestone with operation in city mall Courtney Kruk April 30, 2026 — 4:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A group of armed and uniformed police officers, their fingers looped around their vests, stand at the edge of Queen Street Mall in the heart of Brisbane’s CBD, scanning passersby with intent. One of the first to be stopped, a man in a flannel shirt and long work pants, crouches as a semicircle of officers instruct him to empty the contents of his backpack. Another in similar garb has his socks and pockets turned out at a nearby bench. A man wearing reflective sunglasses and wielding a two-litre bottle of Ice Break is steered towards a garden bed, his belongings laid out next to budding marigolds. Queensland Police officers conduct a wanding operation in Queen Street Mall on Thursday morning. Courtney Kruk An older guy in a Mickey Mouse crew neck and red sneakers submits to a small black handheld device with his arms raised, then offers a sardonic “yeah, yeah, good work guys” as he shuffles away.



A tall accented man in a grey hoodie looks confused by the sudden attention, and attempts to dodge the party of waiting officers. A long interrogation ensues, and he is eventually escorted from the precinct for public nuisance, but not before taking a prayer stance at their feet. Two teenage boys smile as officers wave a metal detector wand over their bodies, offering encouraging handshakes before trailing off towards the old Treasury building. Jack’s Law grants police powers to stop and wand people in public places without a warrant. Courtney Kruk Nearby, Queensland Police Minister Dan Purdie spoke of a significant milestone in Jack’s Law, legislation that allows police to use handheld metal detectors (“wands”) to search individuals in public places without a warrant. The laws are named in honour of 17-year-old Jack Beasley who was fatally stabbed during a night out with friends in Surfers Paradise in 2019, and were expanded and made permanent by the Crisafulli government last year.



Since then, nearly 127,600 scans have been carried out by Queensland police, with over 1000 weapons including machetes, knives and axes seized. Related Article Exclusive

Queensland Police Revealed: The hotspots where people in the crowd are hiding weapons “We never know what those weapons individually would have been used for,” Purdie said. “[But] this is another example of what we’re doing to drive down crime and keep our community safe.” Based on the latest data, Jack’s Law has a detection rate of about 0.81 per cent. On top of the 1032 weapons seized, wanding efforts have led to nearly 2000 arrests and more than 3770 charges. Previous analysis showed the majority of charges tended to be for minor drug offences, or breaches of knife-carrying bans.



Advocates have long called for police to undertake specialised wanding training, and for transparent data collection on who they stop, including age, gender and cultural background, while noting a lack of evidence that the laws reduce violent crime. Jack Beasley’s father Brett, who has channelled the rage and grief of losing a child to a senseless crime into reform, described the milestone announced on Thursday as something he and wife Belinda “couldn’t be prouder of”. Police Minister Dan Purdie, Brett Beasley and Gold Coast Sergeant Mick Chalmers show a wanding device. Courtney Kruk “We’re hoping to [make] Jack’s Law a national law around Australia, to have every single police officer in the country to have the same powers as our Queensland police do,” Brett said. “Every knife off the street is a life saved, as far as we’re concerned.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Tried to build the Taj Mahal with budget for a granny flat’: Demons’ Caulfield deadline revealed
World.content:
Exclusive SportRacingAFL 2026 ‘Tried to build the Taj Mahal with budget for a granny flat’: Demons’ Caulfield deadline revealed Danny Russell April 30, 2026 — 4:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The head of the government-appointed trust that manages the site proposed for Melbourne Football Club’s Caulfield Racecourse development has criticised the Demons for wanting to build a “Taj Mahal” home base with a “budget for a granny flat”. This masthead can reveal the Demons have been given a 60-day deadline to prove they can fund the $100 million training centre or the Caulfield Racecourse Reserve Trust will look for alternative tenants. Melbourne captain Max Gawn leads the Demons on the field at the MCG. via Getty Images This follows the shock dismissal of Melbourne chief executive Paul Guerra on Tuesday after only seven months in the job. Guerra, who previously headed the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, was seen as a key figure in the Demons’ search for a new training and administration centre because of his state government connections and his role as a Racing Victoria board member.



Melbourne president Steven Smith was asked about the status of the Caulfield plans after the Guerra axing on Wednesday. “We’re getting very close on Caulfield; we’re confident on Caulfield,” said Smith, who also announced the appointment of a new club CEO, Dan Taylor. Loading However, trust chairman Sam Almaliki told this masthead the onus was on Melbourne to deliver a commitment of “funding to the project”. “The one critical piece that is beyond the trust’s role and responsibility in this is the funding required to make the project a reality,” Almaliki said.



“The critical vitamin that’s missing is ‘vitamin M’ [money], and Melbourne have not been able to deliver that to date. “The truth is, they’ve tried to build the Taj Mahal, and so far they’ve only got budget for a granny flat.” An artist’s impression of the proposed Melbourne training and administration facility at Caulfield Racecourse. A source familiar with the situation, who declined to be named because the process is confidential, said Melbourne’s memorandum of understanding with the racecourse trust was extended until June 30 this year “for Melbourne to make sure that the project is feasible and that it’s got the financial backing”. This masthead reported in June last year that Melbourne was expected to provide $15 million from cash reserves and $15 million in a fundraising drive, but needed to convince the state and federal governments and the AFL to contribute the remaining $70 million.



A Melbourne Racing Club source told this masthead the racing club (which runs the track) had been dealing with the Melbourne board and not Guerra for some time, but they did not have an issue with the former CEO.



The MRC insider, who was not authorised to speak publicly, said the racing club could not see a future in which the Demons had a home base at Caulfield. Departed Melbourne CEO Paul Guerra. Joe Armao Melbourne Football Club and the state government have been contacted for comment. The Demons had requested a longer extension to the MOU with the trust, but that was denied. “From the trust’s perspective, if the Demons in working with government and other stakeholders cannot demonstrate that Caulfield is feasible and has the financial backing needed, this project is dead in its tracks,” a source said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Guerra was appointed last April. It didn’t take long for the Demons to get buyer’s remorse Almaliki, who has been chair since the trust’s inception in 2018, wrote to Premier Jacinta Allen this week, reinstating the trust’s commitment to the project and welcoming its prioritisation by the government. “The trust continues to collaborate with the Melbourne Football Club, the state government, the Melbourne Racing Club and other stakeholders to deliver a training and administration facility for the Demons at Caulfield,” he said. “Our commitment has not changed and has been consistent. It is now up to all other parties to deliver, to make this happen. That includes the Melbourne Football Club as the party that is looking to call Caulfield home.” Almaliki would not comment on Guerra’s role while at the Demons or on the club’s decision to move him on.



He said it was the trust, with support from the previous Melbourne Racing Club administration, who first approached the Demons about relocating to Caulfield. “The trust’s interest is in delivering community benefit through improved access and activity at Caulfield for everyone,” he said. “Throughout the journey, we’ve taken every opportunity to remove any obstacles in the way of making this possible. “The one outstanding component that nobody has been able to deliver is a commitment of funding to the project. And really the onus rests on the Demons to deliver that. Everything else can be worked through.” The source said the trust asked the Demons and then CEO Gary Pert late in 2024 to start building football fields inside the racecourse to show their commitment to the project, and to prove their intent to potential donors.

World.title: Paramedics ‘scared to go to work’ after colleague attacked
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Paramedics ‘scared to go to work’ after colleague attacked Alexander Darling April 30, 2026 — 4:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paramedics in Victoria are in shock after a passer-by stabbed one of their colleagues in the face and neck while he was on duty on Thursday. The victim, a 20-year professional originally from the Northern Territory, is in Royal Melbourne Hospital’s emergency department in a serious but stable condition after the incident, which happened in Melbourne’s north about 11.20am. Ambulance Victoria chief executive Jordan Emery addressed the media with union secretary Danny Hill (right) and other paramedics on Thursday. Alexander Darling Police and Ambulance Victoria said the first responder was getting coffee at a cafe in Reservoir just after 11am, when a man got out of a red car and stabbed him. The man then fled in the same car, they said. Police made an arrest in the same suburb a few hours later.



The paramedic’s injuries were not life-threatening, but Ambulance Victoria chief executive Jordan Emery said that made the situation no less serious. Related Article Exclusive

Crime ‘An absolute let-down’: Paramedics furious over assault law loophole Speaking outside the Royal Melbourne Hospital on Thursday afternoon, Emery said: “It is completely unacceptable that those people who spend their lives caring for others, who give so much to care for their communities, continue to face violence on a daily basis. “We need to spend time in our communities reflecting on how we have come to a place where more than 1000 paramedics are assaulted every single year in Victoria.” He said the problem was increasing across Victoria and that drug and alcohol abuse weren’t the only explanations.



“There will be paramedics tonight who will be scared to go to work, and rightly so, because of this appalling violence,” he said. Emery said a bystander had intervened to stop the offender, which allowed the paramedic to perform first aid on himself – despite bleeding profusely – until his colleagues arrived. “We extend our sincere gratitude and thanks to that bystander,” Emery said. “We hope that we get the opportunity to provide a more fulsome thanks directly.” Police arrested a 32-year-old man over the incident at a different street in Reservoir at 1pm. The man is being interviewed. Since 2018, injuring an emergency worker has been a category 1 offence in Victoria, meaning courts must impose a prison sentence – in this case at least six months – for those found guilty. The maximum penalty for this crime is five years in jail.



Danny Hill, secretary of Victoria’s Ambulance Union, said the incident demonstrated the need for the state’s leaders to take action. “Until it stops, we’re going to keep advocating for improvements to laws, tighter penalties, harsher penalties,” he said, though he declined to detail what these desired improvements were when asked. World.title: The tuna chilli sanger (with hash brown) that’s autumn’s best comfort food
World.content:
Eating outSandwich Watch The tuna chilli sanger (with hash brown) that’s autumn’s best comfort food You’ll have to negotiate the Upper Mount Gravatt backstreets, crisscrossing the highway a couple of times, to find one. But boy is it worth it. Matt Shea April 30, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The most popular sandwich at Sincerity at Jacorey? Co-owner Corey Park dutifully points at the menu on the counter: the ebi katsu sando, he suggests. Or perhaps the bulgogi sando. Or maybe it’s the chilli karaage sando. All are a hit with Sincerity’s regular clientele. I’m here to tell you, though, that Sincerity’s regular clientele are wrong – if only a little bit. Sincerity by Jacorey’s chilli tuna mayo sandwich Markus Ravik All are fine sandwiches that I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend. Still, they’re all outshone by a chilli tuna mayo number that’s this autumn’s best comfort food. Here’s why. Actually, first, a little about Sincerity by Jacorey



Park and partner Jamie Kim opened their first cafe, Jacorey Dessert Cafe, in early 2024 and soon followed it with Sincerity by Jacorey. Park tends to work front of house on the coffee machine, while Kim oversees the kitchen. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article Riverside Italian classic rebooted for new generation The early focus at both cafes was handcrafted desserts such as a range of Basque cheesecakes, alongside cream lattes and iced matcha. It was only later that Kim developed a range of savoury sandwiches. They’ve since become some of the two cafes’ best-selling items. Sincerity by Jacorey is in Upper Mt Gravatt and is a funny spot to get to. It’s slotted into the ground floor of a pair of apartment blocks perched half a block back from the intersection of Logan and Kessells roads. To get there, you jump off the M1 at Klumpp Road and then wend your way through the backstreets, crossing the freeway a couple of times. Sincerity by Jacorey occupies a comfortably nondescript spot beneath an apartment building in Upper Mount Gravatt. Markus Ravik



It’s an unusual location but a pleasant one, protected from the traffic that thunders along Logan Road. Outside, there are a few tables gathered around a garden bed; the inside is dominated by a communal timber table, with counter seating looking out through floor to ceiling windows. Sincerity by Jacorey’s chilli tuna mayo sandwich What initially attracted us to this brilliant sandwich was – counterintuitively, perhaps – its relative practicality when compared to its more Instagrammable stablemates (the ebi katsu, in particular, is a real peacock of a sanger). But that restraint makes sense when Kim tells you how it came about. Inside Sincerity by Jacorey. Markus Ravik “I have this vivid memory of a spicy tuna [toastie] my sister once made,” she says. “Even though I usually can’t handle spicy food, it was that perfect kind of addictive spicy. I’ve been craving it lately so I decided to recreate it using our chewy sando bread.”



This thing is far more than a tuna toastie, though. Kim mixes skipjack tuna with kewpie mayo and a bunch of spices to create the silky chilli tuna mix at the heart of the sandwich (“[Skipjack] has richer flavour and better texture than albacore,” she says). That’s layered into the sandwich with rocket, honey mustard, tasty cheese and, most importantly, a piping hot Edgell hash brown that Kim chose for its crisp outer shell. The chilli tuna mayo sandwich alongside some of the cafe’s other popular sangers. Markus Ravik Then there’s the sando bread that the ingredients come slapped between, which Kim chose after testing “countless” other brands. She won’t be drawn on where she gets it from but says its “chewy but soft” texture provides the sandwich’s punctuation mark, especially when lightly toasted as it is here. The perfect comfort food



Yes, this thing has way more going on than that toastie Kim’s sister made all those years ago, but the DNA is the same. It’s brilliant, soul-warming comfort food. Its combination of texture and flavour, and then the interplay of temperature, so thoughtful and precise it’s like you’re sitting in on Kim’s own nostalgia. It’s manageable – you can eat it in one hand – but I often find myself eating it with two, elbows on the table, much like I used to when sitting at the kitchen counter as a kid, lost in daydreams. Markus Ravik It’s manageable – you can eat it in one hand – but I often find myself eating it with two, elbows on the table, much like I used to when sitting at the kitchen counter as a kid, lost in daydreams. Where to get it Sincerity by Jacorey’s chilli tuna mayo sandwich is $23.50. You can get one at 5 Cremin Street, Upper Mount Gravatt.

The campaign follows up on historical rock chip samples that returned up to 17.95 grams per tonne gold. Additionally, Dalaroo has completed channel sampling at its Dingbi artisanal site to guide future drilling beneath existing surface workings. Dalaroo is also keeping boots on the ground back on home soil. At its Namban project in Western Australia’s northern wheatbelt, the company is chasing nickel, copper and platinum group elements. Notably, the project sits within the same geological setting as Chalice Mining’s massive 30-million-ounce palladium equivalent Julimar discovery, located just 80 kilometres to the south. Meanwhile, at the Lyons River project in the Gascoyne region, the company is hunting a diverse mineral bounty across an expansive 838-square-kilometre holding, with gold leading the charge. With the core Greenland tenure now locked in, Dalaroo has launched a structured de-risking program for the 2026 field season. The multi-pronged campaign will feature maiden drilling designed to define coherent mineralised zones alongside a suite of high-tech geophysical tools.



Specialised ground-penetrating radar will be deployed to map sediment thickness and identify buried “paleochannels” that could act as heavy mineral traps. In the lagoon itself, the company plans to use side-scan sonar for bathymetry and Van Veen grab sampling to retrieve seabed sediments for mineralogical analysis. By consolidating its hold on the high-grade core and simultaneously applying for massive offshore extensions, Dalaroo is acquiring the ground to potentially define a major new critical minerals province. With a 2026 exploration blitz about to kick off and as the scramble to secure the rare earths for permanent magnets continues, the company’s Greenland discovery is looking more and more like very well-timed piece of potential “company making” geological detective work. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au
